record.original_question: How can standard Einstein gravity solve or avoid the cosmological constant problem if its starting action is not selected by a principle that excludes a cosmological constant term? Equivalently, is an additional invariance principle needed to remove the ambiguity in the gravitational action and prevent a cosmological constant term from appearing at the input Lagrangian level?

evidence.quote: Beyond the phenomenological issue of what relativistic theory is mandated by non-relativistic observation, the standard theory comes with a few other loose ends.

Specifically, since no principle was offered which would uniquely select out the Einstein-Hilbert action (to thus make the above discussion necessary as well as sufficient), no principle was offered which would exclude a possible cosmological constant term, and indeed since its inception Einstein gravity has been plagued by the cosmological constant problem.

First, the starting conformal symmetry not only unambiguously specifies the action (Eq. (2) is the unique conformally invariant action) but by doing so it thereby automatically excludes any cosmological constant term at all at the level of the input Lagrangian.

Thus it appears to us that the origin of the cosmological constant problem in the standard theory may be traced back to an insufficiently motivated choice of starting action, with the Einstein theory simply lacking an additional invariance principle which would remove all ambiguity.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the classical theory of gravity in four spacetime dimensions formulated through a diffeomorphism-invariant action principle on a pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M, g). The Einstein–Hilbert action S_EH = (1/16πG) ∫_M (R − 2Λ) √(−g) d^4x depends on a free parameter Λ, the cosmological constant, because diffeomorphism invariance alone permits the addition of an arbitrary multiple of ∫_M √(−g) d^4x to the gravitational Lagrangian. The cosmological constant problem refers to the fact that no symmetry of the standard theory forbids a Λ term in the input Lagrangian, while observation requires its effective value to be extremely small (or zero).

Question: Within classical Einstein gravity (i.e. without invoking quantum effects or matter cancellation mechanisms), is it possible to solve or avoid the cosmological constant problem if the starting gravitational action is not selected by a principle that intrinsically excludes a cosmological constant term? Equivalently, formulate and justify an additional geometric invariance principle on (M, g) — beyond diffeomorphism invariance — that uniquely determines the gravitational action and rules out any ∫_M Λ √(−g) d^4x term at the level of the input Lagrangian, or prove that no such purely classical invariance principle can do so while remaining consistent with the standard Newtonian and post-Newtonian limits.
artifact.status_search_result: The cosmological constant problem is widely regarded as one of the major unresolved problems of theoretical physics, with numerous proposed approaches (e.g. conformal/Weyl gravity, unimodular gravity, supersymmetric cancellations) but no broadly accepted classical resolution. It remains open as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Cosmological constant problem
status_evidence.snippet: The cosmological constant problem... remains one of the major unsolved problems in physics.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is generally acknowledged as unsolved.

status_evidence.title: The Cosmological Constant Problem (Weinberg)
status_evidence.snippet: Classic review identifying the cosmological constant problem; subsequent decades of work have not produced a consensus solution.
status_evidence.claim: No accepted resolution exists in classical or quantum gravity.
